repository.name: smart-grid-storage-playbook
repository.title: Smart Grid Storage Constraints Lab
repository.description: Explore grid services through BESS power, energy, reserve, frequency, voltage & capability constraints with worked labs.
repository.summary: The playbook pairs concept notes with executable storage and grid-support constraints. The browser begins with active-power balance before directing the learner to native energy, P–Q, ramp, reserve, and derating models.
repository.audience: Power-system students, BESS engineers, and project teams reviewing grid-service assumptions.

model.equation: solar = S · max(0, sin(π(t−6)/12)); demand = D · (0.8 + 0.18 cos(2π(t−19)/24) + 0.12 exp(−((t−19)/3)²)); import = max(demand−solar−battery, 0).
assumptions: An idealized clear-day profile represents one 24-hour period.
Battery discharge is a fixed external power contribution; energy inventory and charge scheduling are omitted.
Solar share is capped at 100%; exports are not credited; grid carbon intensity is constant.
Browser power is in kW; native grid-service examples often use MW/MWh. Convert units explicitly before comparison.
The solar-demand shape is synthetic and does not model network frequency, voltage, reactive power, islanding, or grid-forming control.
A fixed battery contribution is a requested screening assumption, not a feasible or approved dispatch command.
model.introduction: This single-bus active-power screen leaves battery inventory and inverter capability unconstrained. The native playbook supplies the missing energy, P–Q, ramp, frequency/voltage, reserve, and temperature constraints.

modules.title: Draw the requested active-power balance
modules.objective: Identify a grid-service request before applying feasibility constraints.
steps: Read the playbook’s model map and active/reactive capability rule.
Apply a 500 kW demand baseline, 600 kW PV peak, and no battery contribution.
Inspect the evening import and identify which missing constraint would matter if storage supplied it.

checkpoints.label: Evening demand supplied by the grid is 550 kW

modules.reflection: Why must a requested active-power service be checked against both energy inventory and inverter apparent-power capability?

modules.title: Keep power and energy headroom separate
modules.objective: Explain why a lower import value does not prove sustained reserve availability.
steps: Add a fixed 100 kW battery contribution while retaining the same demand and PV.
Predict the evening import and calculate the AC energy requested over a 30-minute service.
Read the native energy-limits and reserve-headroom interfaces to identify SOC floors and efficiency terms.

checkpoints.label: Battery contribution reduces evening import to 450 kW

modules.reflection: What would change if the reserve request had to be sustained for two hours instead of thirty minutes?

modules.title: Identify interacting service constraints
modules.objective: Map a stressed balance to the native model that enforces multiple limits.
steps: Use 800 kW baseline demand, 300 kW PV, and an assumed 200 kW battery contribution.
Run the evening case and convert the battery power to MW.
Read grid_support_sequence.py and identify capability, filtering, ramping, temperature, and energy interactions omitted here.
modules.reflection: Why could active-priority and reactive-priority policies deliver different commands for the same requested P and Q?

modules.title: Write a constrained dispatch study
modules.objective: Carry a clear power question into a sequence that can check physical limits.
steps: Apply 500 kW baseline demand, 600 kW PV, 300 kW assumed battery contribution, and 200 g/kWh carbon.
Run and export the requested balance, stating that storage feasibility is unresolved.
Specify a native study with initial/final SOC, duration, efficiencies, P–Q priority, ramp limits, and reserve requirements.

checkpoints.label: Illustrative grid emissions rate is 50 kg/h

modules.reflection: Which source tests could support implementation correctness, and what site or grid-code evidence would still be needed for an operational decision?
